newsitem.title: USA: US businessmen urge Clinton to end trucking freeze.
newsitem.headline: US businessmen urge Clinton to end trucking freeze.

text.p: Representatives of the U.S. trucking, freight shipping and car industries Wednesday urged President Clinton to end a freeze on the crossborder trucking provisions of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

In a letter to Clinton, trade and business associations asked the president to implement NAFTA rules which were delayed one year ago, restricting the movement of trucks over the 2,000-mile (3,000 km) border with Mexico.

"NAFTA was intended to fix a cumbersome, outdated and costly system of moving freight across the Mexican border. It's time to move forward," American Trucking Associations president Thomas Donohue said at a news conference.
Business leaders present at the conference said the freeze was politically motivated, as it was actively sought by the Teamsters truckers union on the eve of an electoral year.

The Teamsters successfully argued for a delay of NAFTA's trucking provisions, charging that Mexico's heavier and older vehicles posed safety and environmental hazards to the four border states, Arizona, California, New Mexico and Texas.
The Teamsters, which represent some 1.4 million members in the United States and Canada, supported neither Clinton nor his Republican contender, Bob Dole in the Nov. 5 election.
Donohue, who argued that the implementation delay was based on unsupported claims, said the U.S. border states were prepared to enforce U.S. safety regulations.
A spokesman for the union said they still oppose the NAFTA trucking provisions because they threaten highway safety and "good Teamster jobs".
"(The border states) were not ready for it in 1995 and they are not ready today," union spokesman Rand Wilson said.

Over 85 percent of the $120 billion annual trade flows between the United States and Mexico are moved by truck, but due to the freeze U.S. truckers are not allowed to operate in Mexico and Mexican rigs cannot enter U.S. border states.
